This precious head, famed in many tales,
Would have been cut short.”
Sary Khan did not falter;
Saying, “Let my anger break upon stone,”
He seized a black boulder
As massive as Opol-Too and swung it around.
Making the rock ring aloud,
Sary Khan brought his mace down
And struck it with all his force.
Sparks flew from the mace;
The boulder split cleanly and burst apart,
And fire sprang from the black stone.
Lives scattered from beneath it,
And, swaying upon Tootoru,
The mountain-like Kyyaz emerged.
When Sary Khan saw the hero Kyyaz,
He at once leveled
His ornamented spear with its steel shaft,
His ornamented spear with its steel point,*
And thrust it forward with a roar.
Your uncle Sary, ever ready for war,
Took aim at mounted Kyyaz,
At the face of his right shoulder blade,
At the edge of his spinal bone,
At the region of his vital windpipe—
“This is the place where Kyyaz,
The avenger of blood, must die,” he said,
And drove the spear home.
Sary Khan unleashed calamity:
Kyyaz doubled over on Tootoru,
And the huge, mountain-like warrior
Nearly went flying from the saddle.
He slipped backward from the saddle,
His feet came free of the stirrups,
The two fronts of his robe hung loose,
And his two eyes rolled wildly.
Straining in anguish,
Kyyaz, hero of the Jediger,
Despaired now even of his fly-like life.
He sprawled helplessly over Tootoru;
Just as Kyyaz was about to fall,
As Kyyaz, hero of the Jediger,
Clearly reached the hour of his death,
The vigor of youth left him,
His world contracted around him,
And he cried out in fury.
His protector was Kanchoro,
And such was the madman’s nature—
“My comrade!” he cried.
Kanchoro, son of Chubak,
Rode beneath him
Köktelki, the horse of Khan Köbösh.
He wheeled Köktelki around—
God had struck the slave with madness.
Thinking Kyyaz would tumble
From Tootoru and hit the earth,
And that Sary the Bald, who had done so much,
Would needlessly reach his side,
Cut off his head,
And bring about his death,
The raging slave seized sharp steel
And came charging up.
The scoundrel struck Sary Khan’s spear
Across the middle of its shaft
And chopped it clean in two.
Then Sary Khan realized
That Kanchoro was the enemy.
Your uncle’s heart constricted;
Looking neither up nor down,
With a roar that split stone,
And sparing not his life from death,
He began the joyous carnage,
Binding his miserable, mangy life
To a single hair and casting it away.
Looking at nothing around him,
Sary Khan proved steadfast,
Never sparing his life.
Damn you, treacherous slave,
Who forgot every honor and custom,
Wicked son who pisses in the cauldron!
This Sultan Semetey
Kept you beside him and made you a hero,
And made you equal to the sons of warriors.
He raised you from childhood,
And set your wretched life aright.
He hung upon your arm
A keen sword, sharp when drawn;
He gave you command over the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
So none would stir without your knowing;
He let you ride
Over the foes who faced you;
He had ninety beasts slaughtered for your feast.
Hoping you would become a father to the people,
Would slay the enemy who fought you,
Would display true valor,
And shield the Kyrgyz
From every calamity and malicious word,
He deliberately gave you a name fit for a khan
And called you Kanchoro.
Swaying, a hero no enemy could break—
He made an iron-fenced fortress,
Renowned throughout the world,
And made you, Kanchoro, a lord.
From the fat-tailed sheep and the mare
He carved the finest meat and fed you;
Saying, “You shall be like my own brother,”
At his mother’s breast
He let you suckle, treacherous son.
Before all the countless people
Whose ears had heard and eyes had seen,
When did he ever let anyone call you a child of misfortune?
He had your belt bound firmly;
The Six Cities and Margalan,
All the way to Kokand and Samarkand—
He made them all submit,
And had you exact the blood-price for your father Chubak.
Calling it “Chubak’s unpayable blood-price,”
The multitude clamored and wept in anguish;
Most of the Uyghurs and Margalan,
All the people who witnessed it, wept.
Kanchoro raised you well;
Your father’s noble Semetey—
It was my Kanchoro who fostered you.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
Ah, my son Kanchoro,
Your mind is shallow and your heart is foul;
You fired upon your own elder brother—
There is no fool like you in all the world.
Your mighty, thundering mother’s
Silver has turned to charcoal;
You have grown arrogant, Kanchoro,
Fattening without knowing the pain of burning grief.
The fierce wolf, the son of Manas—
His gold has turned to charcoal;
You brought calamity and strife upon his head.
Damn you, Kanchoro,
For fattening without knowing what you received!
These were the words Kanykey once spoke:
“Ah, that wretched woman was a seer;
In the end, may he perish,
She said he would prove no true kinsman.”
Affairs collapsed and conflict broke out;
The fierce, heroic Kanykey—
The poor woman’s words came true!
Had I heeded Kanykey’s words
Yesterday, at Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
When the Kyrgyz lay spread across the land,
When you were still in your cradle,
Why did I not gouge out
Your blackcurrant eyes?
Why did I not seize you, put you to the sword,
And slaughter you?
Before you began your wicked schemes,
You rabid cur,
Why did I not finish you for good?
Our blood and judgment failed us—
Old Bakay and all of us.
My son, posing as a younger brother,
You were only narrowing your eyes in deceit;
It turns out that all along
You were our enemy.
You thought, “I have enjoyed Semetey’s glory;
Now I shall destroy him.”
Through all your treachery, you thought,
“I shall bring him to his end.”
You forsook your own borders, you madman,
And thought you would go
To the people of Jediger.
You will not dwell in Jeti-Özön;
You fired upon your own elder,
And since your very origin is accursed,
You will find no refuge among the Jediger!
You will not camp along the hillsides;
Since your guide is evil,
Your end will never prosper!”
So spoke Sary Khan,
His eyes darkening and seething,
His broad teeth, like rows of pegs,
Grinding against one another like millet.
His whole breast was fire and flame;
Unable to endure it, Sary Khan
Glowered and bristled,
His full courage rising like fur,
Rumbling as he broke away,
Looking like a gray lion—
Such was his fearsome aspect.
Taking up the red, mist-like banner,
Taking a tufted spear with a barbed blade,
And girding on his unsheathed sword—
Such was his prowess—
He prayed to the Creator:
“O soulless Jediger,
I shall mount my bannered charger;
Without regarding him as kin,
I shall drive this dog in every direction!
I shall unleash a storm of gunfire,
And rescue my noble wolf-born prince
From death, calamity,
And torment!”
He tugged and flung aside his mustache,
And tore wildly at his beard;
His whitening beard grew thin,
And, never sparing his life from the beginning,
Tears streamed from his two poor eyes,
Pouring down over his chest.
Making his bannered charger rear,
Sary Khan came into battle,
Destroying all who crossed his path.
Every ridge rang with cries;
The teeming countless host—
Mighty Sary Khan
Drove them back in confusion.
He routed them without leaving one behind
And drove them to the riverbank,
When, from a spur where the mountain vanished,
My broad-backed bay horse looming beneath him,
The slave Kyyaz appeared.
“What wrong have these countless people done?
Is not the khan of this black-hearted rabble
A fool himself?
I shall hew off with an axe
The head of Kyyaz, son of Bagysh;
If any of my former strength remains,
I shall bring such battle upon
This mad fool marked for death
That, turning back from Jeti-Özön,
He will never come again;
I shall fight the villain
And ensure he never returns!
I shall make him unable to cross
The forked pass and barren slope;
I shall make him unable to march
His agitated host through Talas!”
Sary Khan wheeled across his path
And turned his bannered charger’s head;
With his stout and mighty patterned spear,
Aiming straight at brave Kyyaz,
He thundered forward with leveled lance.
At that moment, brave Kyyaz,
When he saw Sary Khan,
Lost the strength in his wrists,
And the courage in his heart;
His ribs trembled,
And, unable to endure it, brave Kyyaz
Felt his fly-like soul quiver.
His strength failed and his power deserted him;
Over a saddle-shaped ridge
Brave Kyyaz fled,
Keeping beyond your uncle Sary’s reach;
Brave Kyyaz escaped,
Despairing of his precious life,
His face drained of color.
To the hero Kanchoro
Brave Kyyaz came alive.
